newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Randgold Resources plans LSE debut June 30.
newsitem.headline: Randgold Resources plans LSE debut June 30.

text.p: Randgold Resources, the African gold mining and exploration company, said on Thursday it planned to start trading on the London Stock Exchange on June 30, parent company Randgold and Exploration Co said.

"An international offer of approximately seven million new shares and global depositary securities is being led by HSBC Investment Bank. The target date for unconditional dealings in RRL shares and GDSs to start on the LSE is 30 June 1997," it said.

Randgold said that RRL (Randgold Resources Ltd) had reached the stage where its strategic development required a substantial capital injection with funding required for the development of existing projects, notably the Syama gold mine and Loulo project in Mali.

Other more advanced exploration projects including Golden Ridge in Tanzani, Morila in Mali, Nielle in Cote d'Ivoire and Sanmatenga in Burkino Faso also required funding. The money would also support the acquisition of gold mines and projects in sub-Saharan Africa.
Randgold said it could not supply RRL with this financing directly due to the constraints imposed by the South African exchange control system.
"The directors believe the most effective way of facilitating this is to combine the raising of capital with a listing on the London Stock Exchange...," RRL's preliminary listing circular said.
"In addition, the nature and extent of RRL's interests in sub-Saharan Africa have led the directors to a London listing as the most appropriate structure for the RRL group."
The necessary applications for the listing are currently being made.
The listing circular said that RRL's growth strategy included discovering bulk tonnage shallow deposits with the potential to produce at least one million ounces of gold per site.
It would acquire underperforming mines, improving them with RRL's expertise.
In the short term RRL would look to develop the Loulo project and make a mining decision on at least one other project in the next 24 months.
In the longer term, it aimed to bring a new property into production every 18 months to two years.
